text: Computers find each other by numeric IP addresses, not names, so when you type a web address into your browser, a lookup called DNS resolution translates the name into an IP address. The browser checks its own cache first, in case it looked up the domain recently. If it has a saved answer, it uses it and skips everything else. If it doesn't, the request goes to a recursive resolver. That's a server usually run by your internet provider or by a public DNS service. The resolver moves down the naming hierarchy one level at a time. It starts with a root server, which points it to the top-level domain (TLD) server for the right ending, such as ".com". The TLD server sends it to the authoritative server for that particular domain, and that server returns the actual IP address. The resolver hands the address back to your browser. Both of them cache it for a set period called the time to live (TTL), which is often 300 seconds (five minutes). That's a compromise between speed and freshness. If you go back to the site, it loads quickly, and if the address changes, the new one spreads soon after.
